questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with iron deficiency anemia?

options.text: Fatigue, pallor, spoon-shaped nails and a low ferritin
Beefy red tongue and numbness in the feet
Ruddy skin and itching after a hot shower

rationale.correct: Iron deficiency: microcytic anemia, low ferritin, fatigue, pallor and koilonychia.

perOption.a: Low iron stores reduce hemoglobin production.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which instruction should the nurse give a client starting oral ferrous sulfate?

options.text: "Take it with orange juice, and expect your stools to be dark."
"Stop taking it if your stools turn dark."

rationale.correct: Oral iron: take with vitamin C, separate from dairy and antacids, use a straw for liquid forms, expect dark stools and prevent constipation.

perOption.a: Vitamin C improves absorption, and dark stools are harmless.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with pernicious anemia is receiving vitamin B12 injections. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll need these injections for the rest of my life."
"I'll only need the injections until I feel better."
"The tingling in my feet may improve."

rationale.correct: Pernicious anemia: lack of intrinsic factor means lifelong B12 replacement (injections, or high-dose oral or nasal forms if prescribed).

perOption.a: Lack of intrinsic factor is permanent.
perOption.b: B12 replacement is lifelong because the client can't absorb it from food.
perOption.c: Neurologic symptoms can improve with treatment.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach about lifelong vitamin B12 therapy.

questions.stem: Which finding suggests vitamin B12 deficiency rather than iron deficiency?

options.text: Smooth, beefy red tongue and tingling in the hands and feet

rationale.correct: B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia with neurologic signs.

perOption.a: B12 is needed for nerve function, so neurologic symptoms point to B12 deficiency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell B12 deficiency apart from iron deficiency.

questions.stem: Which client is at highest risk for folic acid deficiency anemia?

options.text: A client with long-term heavy alcohol use
A client who eats leafy green vegetables daily
A client taking a prenatal vitamin

rationale.correct: Folate deficiency is linked to alcohol use, poor diet, pregnancy and some medications.

perOption.a: Alcohol impairs folate absorption, and the diet is often poor.
perOption.b: Leafy greens are rich in folate.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify risk factors for folate deficiency.

questions.stem: A client is admitted in sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis. Which interventions are the priority?

options.text: IV fluids, oxygen if hypoxic and opioid pain relief

rationale.correct: Sickle cell crisis: hydration, pain control, oxygen if needed, warmth and treatment of triggers.

perOption.a: Hydration reduces sickling, and severe pain needs prompt opioids.
perOption.b: Cold causes vasoconstriction and more sickling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care in sickle cell crisis.

questions.stem: Which factors can trigger a sickle cell crisis and should be avoided? Select all that apply.

rationale.correct: Prevent crises by staying hydrated and warm, avoiding low oxygen and treating infections early.

perOption.a: Low fluid volume increases sickling.
perOption.b: Infection increases metabolic demand and sickling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach prevention of sickle cell crises.

questions.stem: A client with sickle cell disease has chest pain, fever, an oxygen saturation of 88% and a new infiltrate on chest x-ray. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Acute chest syndrome: chest pain, fever, hypoxia and a new infiltrate. It needs oxygen, antibiotics, pain control and possibly transfusion.

perOption.a: This is a life-threatening complication that needs urgent treatment.
perOption.b: Hypoxia with a new infiltrate isn't simple crisis pain.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with sickle cell disease takes hydroxyurea. Which laboratory test is most important to monitor?

rationale.correct: Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin but can cause myelosuppression; monitor the CBC.

perOption.a: Hydroxyurea suppresses the bone marrow.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with sepsis is oozing blood from IV sites and has petechiae. The platelets are 40,000/mm3, the fibrinogen is low and the D-dimer is high. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: DIC: low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and aPTT, high D-dimer. Treat the cause and replace blood products.

perOption.a: Widespread clotting uses up platelets and clotting factors, causing bleeding.
perOption.b: This doesn't cause these lab findings.
perOption.c: Hemophilia is inherited and has normal platelets.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has received heparin for 6 days, and the platelet count has dropped from 240,000 to 95,000/mm3. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Stopping all heparin, including flushes, and starting a non-heparin anticoagulant

rationale.correct: HIT: platelets fall by more than 50% after 5 to 10 days of heparin. Stop all heparin and use argatroban or another non-heparin agent.

perOption.a: This suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which carries a high risk of clotting.
perOption.c: Platelets may worsen clotting in HIT.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's platelet count is 18,000/mm3. Which bleeding precautions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply pressure for at least 5 minutes after needle removal

rationale.correct: Thrombocytopenia: prevent trauma, avoid antiplatelet drugs and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: This prevents cuts.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with hemophilia A has a painful, swollen knee after a minor fall. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply ice, immobilize and elevate the knee, and give factor VIII as prescribed

rationale.correct: Hemarthrosis: RICE and factor replacement; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.

perOption.a: This controls bleeding into the joint.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage bleeding into a joint in hemophilia.

questions.stem: A client with polycythemia vera has a high hematocrit. Which treatment should the nurse expect?

rationale.correct: Polycythemia vera: phlebotomy, hydration, and watching for clots and bleeding.

perOption.a: Removing blood lowers its thickness and the risk of clots.
perOption.c: This raises the red cell count further.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: How should the nurse run a unit of packed red blood cells?

options.text: Start slowly for the first 15 minutes while watching closely, and finish within 4 hours
Infuse it as fast as possible
Refrigerate it on the unit until needed

rationale.correct: Packed RBCs: start slowly, complete within 4 hours and monitor closely.

perOption.a: Most severe reactions happen early, and longer infusions raise bacterial risk.
perOption.c: Fast early rates make a reaction worse.
perOption.d: Blood is kept in the blood bank refrigerator only.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Infuse packed red blood cells safely.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old with heart failure is receiving a second unit of blood. The client becomes short of breath, with crackles and a blood pressure of 172/96 mm Hg. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: TACO: stop the transfusion, sit the client upright, give oxygen and anticipate a diuretic. Prevent it by infusing slowly.

perOption.a: Volume overload in a client with limited cardiac reserve causes pulmonary edema and hypertension.
perOption.b: This causes fever, back pain and hypotension.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: During a transfusion, a client develops mild hives and itching with stable vital signs. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stop the transfusion and notify the provider; an antihistamine may be given and the transfusion restarted per order
Continue the transfusion at a faster rate

rationale.correct: Every reaction starts with stopping the transfusion; only mild allergic reactions may resume after treatment.

perOption.a: Mild allergic reactions may allow restarting the transfusion after an antihistamine, per the provider.
perOption.c: The unit is held until the provider decides.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a mild allergic transfusion reaction.

questions.stem: A client who is a Jehovah's Witness has anemia and declines blood products. Which alternative might the nurse discuss with the provider?

options.text: Asking the family to override the refusal

rationale.correct: Respect the refusal; alternatives include ESAs, iron, volume expanders and blood-conservation techniques.

perOption.a: These raise hemoglobin without transfusion.
perOption.b: A competent client's refusal must be respected.
perOption.c: The family can't override a competent adult.
perOption.d: This is also a blood product.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Advocate for alternatives when a client refuses blood.

questions.stem: For each complete blood count result, select the interpretation.

rationale.correct: Know the CBC reference ranges and follow the facility's values.

perOption.b1:a: Normal is about 12 to 16 g/dL for adult females.
perOption.b1:b: The result is low, not within normal range.
perOption.b1:c: The result is low, not high.
perOption.b2:a: The result is high, not low.
perOption.b2:b: The result is high, not within normal range.
perOption.b3:a: The result is within normal range, not low.
perOption.b3:c: The result is within normal range, not high.

references: Laboratory reference ranges as used in common NCLEX review texts; follow the facility's ranges
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is receiving IV iron dextran for the first time. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give a test dose and watch for anaphylaxis, with emergency equipment ready
Mix it with the client's blood transfusion

rationale.correct: Iron dextran carries a risk of anaphylaxis; newer IV irons have lower risk but still need monitoring.

perOption.a: Iron dextran can cause anaphylaxis.
perOption.c: Medications are never added to blood.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with thalassemia receives frequent transfusions. Which medication should the nurse expect to prevent iron overload?

rationale.correct: Chelation therapy (deferoxamine or deferasirox) prevents iron overload from repeated transfusions.

perOption.a: Deferoxamine binds excess iron so it can be excreted.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with septic shock is being monitored for disseminated intravascular coagulation. Highlight the findings that suggest DIC.

segments.text: Oozing blood from the IV site and around the arterial line
Petechiae on the chest and arms

rationale.correct: DIC causes clotting and bleeding at the same time.

perOption.s1: Consumption of clotting factors causes bleeding from puncture sites.
perOption.s5: Small clots reduce blood flow to the extremities.
perOption.s7: Fever reflects the sepsis rather than DIC.
perOption.s9: Bleeding into the urine suggests a coagulopathy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the clinical signs of DIC.
